```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

A model reads a long document in pieces, called *chunks*, and the chunking
decides what it sees together. Put a figure in one chunk and the sentence that
explains it in the next, and the model may never read them side by side. This
guide covers the nine ways harnessr cuts a document, the settings all nine
share, and how to compare chunkings before you pay for any reading.

Six of the nine segmenters make no model calls. A seventh makes none by
default. At their defaults, you can try all seven for nothing.
`vignette("harnessr")` introduces the package and the ideas this guide uses,
and `vignette("ingest")` covers the step before this one.

```{r message = FALSE}
library(harnessr)
old <- hr_options(verbose = FALSE, embedder = "lexical")
```

Only one segmenter embeds text: `semantic`. With `embedder = "lexical"` it
uses hashed bag-of-words vectors instead of an embeddings endpoint, so this
guide runs offline and gives the same chunks every time.

## What segmentation produces

`gr_segment()` takes a document from `gr_ingest()` (or anything `gr_ingest()`
accepts) and a segmentation, and returns a chunk set:

```{r}
doc <- gr_ingest(gr_example())
ch <- gr_segment(doc, list(method = "structural", max_tokens = 120))
ch
```

The segmentation can be a segmenter's name, a named list as above, or a
`gr_segment_spec()`. Each chunk records where it came from:

```{r}
ch$chunks[, c("chunk_id", "tokens", "page", "section", "block_id")]
```

`page` is `NA` here because the example is Markdown, which has no pages. A
PDF fills it in. Two other cases also give `NA`:

- `block_id` on a chunk built from several blocks;
- `page` on a chunk that runs from one page onto the next.

A chunk that spans places gets `NA` instead of the first place it touches.
`ans$evidence` reports this provenance for every chunk an answer rests on.

You rarely call `gr_segment()` yourself. `answer_document()` calls it with the
`segment` part of a recipe:

```{r}
gr_recipe("survey")$segment[c("method", "max_tokens", "overlap_tokens")]
```

To change it, build your own recipe with `gr_recipe(segment = list(...))`.
`vignette("readers")` covers recipes.

## The nine segmenters

Each segmenter is a different hypothesis about where meaning breaks:

| segmenter | boundary hypothesis | cost | needs client | provenance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `fixed` | meaning is uniform; cut on a ruler (the control condition) | free | no | none |
| `paragraph` | the author's paragraph breaks are real | free | no | page, section, block |
| `sentence` | sentences are atomic; pack tightly | free | no | page, section, block |
| `recursive` | use the strongest separator that still fits | free | no | none |
| `structural` | headings are boundaries; never merge across sections | free | no | page, section, block |
| `page` | the page is the unit: forms, invoices, scanned records | free | no | page, section, block |
| `semantic` | cut where consecutive embeddings diverge most | 1 embedding pass | yes | page, section, block |
| `contextual` | chunks prefixed with where they sit | free, or 1 call/chunk | only for `context_source = "llm"` | page, section, block |
| `proposition` | rewrite into standalone factual statements | 1 call per ~900-token batch | yes | none |

The cost and client columns are read from the registry, so you can check them
yourself:

```{r}
gr_segmenters()[, c("name", "cost", "needs_client", "calls")]
```

`paragraph` is the default. It packs the author's paragraphs, in order, into
chunks up to the cap. `sentence` packs sentences instead, for more, smaller
chunks with cleaner edges.

`structural` never lets a chunk cross a heading. By default
(`prefix_section = TRUE`) it also starts every chunk with its section's
heading, so the fourth chunk of a long "Methods" section still names its
subject. If the extractor found no sections, `structural` finds headings
itself: a Markdown `#` line, or a short line that is numbered or written in
capitals.

`page` makes one chunk per page. It splits only a page too long for the cap,
and prints a message when it does.

`fixed` cuts the text into windows of equal size and ignores its structure, so
it serves as the baseline for the others. `recursive` splits on the strongest
separator that still gives pieces under the cap. By default the cascade runs
from blank lines to line breaks, then sentence ends, semicolons, commas and
spaces. Set your own cascade, strongest first, with `separators`.

By design, `fixed` and `recursive` work on the whole document joined into one
string, so their chunks carry no page or section. That is the cost of ignoring
structure. harnessr reports it as `NA` instead of guessing:

```{r}
fx <- gr_segment(doc, list(method = "fixed", max_tokens = 120))
fx$chunks[1:3, c("chunk_id", "page", "section", "block_id")]
```

The sections below cover the last three segmenters, `semantic`, `contextual`
and `proposition`, with the settings and model calls they add.

## When a segmenter cannot run as asked

If a segmenter cannot do what you asked, harnessr falls back to one that can,
warns, and records the change. `page` on a source with no page numbers falls
back to `paragraph`:

```{r warning = FALSE}
pg <- gr_segment(doc, "page")
pg$method
```

Without a client, `semantic` falls back to `paragraph` and `proposition` to
`sentence`. The fallback shows in `$method` (`"semantic->paragraph"`,
`"proposition->sentence"`) and in the `method` column of `gr_chunk_stats()`,
so a comparison never reports a chunking that did not run.

`contextual` keeps its name when `context_source = "llm"` has no client,
because only the source of its context lines changed. `$extra$context_source`
records the source that ran, `"metadata"`.

Each of these warnings has the class `gr_segment_fallback`. harnessr carries
the warning onto the answer of any read that uses the chunks.

## Chunk size

`max_tokens` caps a chunk's size. `gr_segment()` holds every segmenter to it,
including one you register yourself. After a segmenter returns, `gr_segment()`
splits any chunk over the cap (at sentences, then words, then characters) and
counts the chunks it split in `$extra$cap_enforced`. Each piece keeps the page,
section and block of its original chunk.

If the active tokenizer counts a single character as more than the cap,
`gr_segment()` stops with an error of class `gr_cap_unenforceable` instead of
sending a chunk the model will reject.

harnessr corrects a setting out of range and warns about the correction:

```{r}
tryCatch(gr_segment_spec("paragraph", max_tokens = 100, overlap_tokens = 500),
         warning = conditionMessage)
```

`max_tokens` is held to between 32 and 1,000,000, `overlap_tokens` to less than
`max_tokens`, and `min_tokens` to no more than `max_tokens`.

The right size depends on the reader. A reader that sends every chunk pays for
each request, so small chunks multiply the bill. A reader that picks the best
few chunks needs chunks small enough that those few hold the answer and little
else. `vignette("readers")` compares the readers.

## Overlap

Without overlap, a boundary can split an answer between two chunks, and
neither chunk may hold enough of it. `overlap_tokens` copies the end of each
chunk into the start of the next. You pay for the duplicated tokens, which
`gr_chunk_stats()` shows as a larger `total_tokens`:

```{r}
do.call(rbind, lapply(c(0, 30, 60), function(ov)
  gr_chunk_stats(gr_segment(doc, list(method = "sentence", max_tokens = 120,
                                      overlap_tokens = ov)))))
```

The document is the same 534 tokens each time. At 60 tokens of overlap the
model would be sent 863, about 60% more.

harnessr cuts the carried text at a sentence boundary when one is close, and
otherwise at a word. Text written without spaces (Chinese, Japanese, Thai) is
cut by characters. The overlap is trimmed so that the chunk it opens still fits
the cap.

Provenance counts the overlap. Say a chunk opens with a sentence carried from
page 3 and goes on to page 4. It reports page `NA`, since it is not wholly from
either.

Overlap applies to every segmenter with two exceptions:

- `page`, where the page is the unit;
- `proposition`, whose statements are written to stand alone, so its overlap
  is always 0.

`structural` applies overlap within a section, never across a heading.

## Minimum size

`min_tokens` merges a chunk smaller than this into the chunk before it, so a
one-line paragraph between two headings does not become a request of its own.
The merge happens only when the result still fits the cap. With a cap of 60
tokens the example's paragraphs give fourteen chunks, the smallest of 8 tokens.
`min_tokens = 30` folds one of them away:

```{r}
do.call(rbind, lapply(c(0, 30), function(m)
  gr_chunk_stats(gr_segment(doc, list(method = "paragraph", max_tokens = 60,
                                      min_tokens = m)))))
```

`fixed` and `page` ignore `min_tokens`. `structural` never merges across
headings, so it applies `min_tokens` within a section only. Its 16-token first
chunk, the report's title, stays as it is whatever you set:

```{r}
gr_chunk_stats(gr_segment(doc, list(method = "structural", max_tokens = 120,
                                    min_tokens = 40)))
```

## Context lines

A chunk retrieved on its own can be hard to place. "It rose 17 percent" means
little without the section it came from. `contextual` packs paragraphs as
`paragraph` does, then starts each chunk with a bracketed line saying where it
sits. By default (`context_source = "metadata"`) harnessr builds the line from
the file name, section, page and position, at no cost:

```{r}
ctx <- gr_segment(doc, list(method = "contextual", max_tokens = 120))
cat(ctx$chunks$text[2])
```

With `context_source = "llm"` a model writes the line instead. Each call
sends the chunk, the document's first 1,500 tokens and the chunk's section
path from the document's headings (`"Report > Results"`), so the model can
place a chunk from deep in a long document. `contextual` makes one request per
chunk and never more: `$extra$cost` declares `calls` and `calls_max` as the
number of chunks. The mock client below stands in for that model:

```{r}
writer <- hr_mock_client(function(messages, params) "This excerpt reports the 2024 results.")
ctx_llm <- gr_segment(doc, list(method = "contextual", max_tokens = 120,
                                context_source = "llm"), client = writer)
cat(ctx_llm$chunks$text[2])
```

Before packing, `contextual` holds back room for the line from each chunk, so
adding the line never pushes a chunk over the cap. The room is:

- for `"llm"`, `context_reply_tokens` (90 by default);
- for `"metadata"`, the longest header the document could need;
- in both cases, never more than half of `max_tokens`.

A line that still does not fit is shortened. The document text is not.

If a context call fails or is skipped at the run's limits, the chunk keeps its
text without a line. `$extra$blurbs_missing` counts those chunks, and a
`gr_segment_fallback` warning reports them.

The context line is not the document's text, and a model may have written it.
The chunk therefore keeps its body alone in a `source_text` column. harnessr
checks a quotation from the chunk against that column, never against the
line:

```{r}
ctx_llm$chunks$source_text[2]
unlist(ctx_llm$extra$cost)
```

## Segmenters that call a model

Three segmenters spend something, and each takes a `client`:

- `semantic` embeds the text a few sentences at a time (`semantic_window`,
  default 2) and cuts where two neighbouring windows differ most. By default
  it cuts at distances above the `semantic_percentile` (default 90; higher
  gives fewer, larger chunks). With `semantic_threshold = "texttiling"` it
  cuts at the deep valleys of the similarity between neighbouring windows
  (see below). The packer then holds the pieces to the cap and the minimum.
- `contextual` with `context_source = "llm"` makes one call per chunk, as
  above.
- `proposition` sends the document in batches of about
  `proposition_batch_tokens` (default 900). The model rewrites each batch into
  standalone factual statements, with pronouns resolved and numbers kept as
  written.

With `proposition_context_tokens` above 0, each `proposition` request also
carries that many tokens from the end of the batch before it, so the model can
resolve what the batch refers back to. The chunks are the model's words, so
`source_text` holds the passage each was written from, and harnessr checks
quotes against that passage. Each chunk keeps the page and section of its
passage. Three counts in `$extra` track what the check and the model did:

- `propositions_unsupported` counts propositions with no support in their
  passage: a number the passage does not give, or most of the words absent.
  With `proposition_check = "drop"`, harnessr also drops each one as invented,
  counts it in `propositions_dropped`, and warns with class
  `gr_proposition_dropped`.
- `batches_kept_as_written` counts batches the model could not rewrite.
  harnessr keeps such a batch as written instead of dropping it, and warns.

```{r}
cl <- hr_mock_client(function(messages, params) "unused")
sem <- gr_segment(doc, list(method = "semantic", max_tokens = 120), client = cl)
gr_chunk_stats(sem)
sem$extra$embedding_source
```

`embedding_source` is `"lexical"` here, so the boundaries follow shared words
instead of meaning, and `$method` says so: `"semantic->lexical"`. With a real
embeddings endpoint, `embedding_source` is `"api"` and the method is
`"semantic"`. The `->lexical` suffix is a label only: it changes neither the
chunks nor the requests.

These requests count against the run's limits, `hr_options(max_calls =,
max_cost_usd =)`, like any other. Called without a `trace`, `gr_segment()`
makes its own and returns it as `$trace`, so you can see what segmenting cost:

```{r}
hr_trace_summary(ctx_llm$trace)[, c("calls", "tokens_in", "tokens_out")]
```

`vignette("runs")` covers limits and traces.

## Comparing segmentations

`gr_chunk_stats()` sums up a chunk set in one row, so you compare chunkings
with `rbind()`:

```{r}
do.call(rbind, lapply(c("fixed", "paragraph", "sentence", "structural"),
  function(m) gr_chunk_stats(gr_segment(doc, list(method = m, max_tokens = 120)))))
```

The columns:

- `n` is the number of chunks, and so the number of requests for a reader that
  sends every chunk.
- `total_tokens` grows with overlap and with text a segmenter adds, such as the
  headings `structural` puts at the top of its chunks.
- `over_cap` is 0 for anything `gr_segment()` returns, since `gr_segment()`
  enforces the cap. The column is there for chunk sets built some other way.
- `method` names any fallback.

To see what different chunkings do to an answer, give `gr_compare()` recipes
that differ only in their `segment`. `gr_compare()` extracts the document once
and reuses a segmentation across recipes whose segment settings match, so you
pay more than once only for the reading:

```{r}
cmp <- gr_compare(gr_example(), "What was revenue?", list(
  gr_recipe("by_paragraph", segment = list(method = "paragraph", max_tokens = 120),
            read = list(reader = "retrieve", top_k = 2)),
  gr_recipe("by_section", segment = list(method = "structural", max_tokens = 120),
            read = list(reader = "retrieve", top_k = 2))), client = cl)
cmp$summary[, c("recipe", "segmenter", "chunks", "reader", "chunks_used")]
```

## Choosing the settings

Each walkthrough below takes one segmentation setting or group of settings
and covers four things:

- what it controls and what it trades off;
- the signs in your results that point to changing it;
- where its default came from;
- how to test a change.

`vignette("settings")` lists every segmentation setting with its default.

Test a chunking first with the free statistics: `gr_chunk_stats()` above, and
`gr_seg_recall()` and `gr_seg_pk()` in `vignette("compare")`. To test what a
chunking does to answers, use arms: `hr_sweep()` builds one arm per value and
`hr_benchmark()` runs them on a reference.

Here the arms run on one question and a stand-in model that always answers
correctly. The examples therefore show how to build and read a sweep; they do
not show which value is better. `vignette("compare")` runs a grid of
segmenters and chunk sizes on dev, then compares one choice on test with
intervals.

```{r}
qa <- gr_qa_reference(questions = c(revenue = "What was revenue in 2024?"),
                      documents = gr_example(), answers = list("45.2 million"),
                      split = "dev")
says <- hr_mock_client(function(messages, params) "Revenue was 45.2 million dollars.")
sweep <- function(arms) {
  hr_benchmark(arms, qa, runs = 5, client = says, split = "dev",
               scorer = gr_scorer_answer())
}
```

### Which segmenter {#set-method}

**What it controls.** `method` sets where the cuts fall: on a ruler (`fixed`),
at the author's paragraphs, sentences or headings, at pages, or where the
embeddings shift (`semantic`). Each is a guess about where meaning breaks. A
cut through the middle of a table or an argument separates parts a model needs
together. Chunks that keep whole sections are larger and fewer.

**Signs it needs changing.** Suspect cuts in the wrong places when an answer
gives half a figure or a quotation stops mid-sentence. Look at the chunks
around it with `chunks$chunks$text`. The same sign, measured, is
`gr_seg_recall()` reporting the answer outside the top chunks for one
segmenter and inside for another. Try `structural` on a document with headings
that a `paragraph` chunking runs across, and `page` on a form or invoice.

**Where the default came from.** `paragraph` was chosen because it needs no
model or embedder. It has not been compared with the others (`untested`).
Each recipe sets its own: `"needle"` uses `semantic`, `"precise"` uses
`sentence`.

**How to test it.** Sweep it on the recipe you use:

```{r}
bench <- sweep(hr_sweep(gr_arm("needle"),
                        list(method = c("paragraph", "sentence", "structural"))))
aggregate(tokens_in ~ param.method, bench, mean)
```

All three arms sent different requests here (`hr_sweep_check(bench)` has no
rows). `structural` sent the most, 690 prompt tokens against 667 for
`sentence`, because its chunks carry their headings.

### Chunk size: `max_tokens` {#set-max-tokens}

**What it controls.** `max_tokens` caps every chunk. Smaller chunks mean more
requests for a reader that sends every chunk. They also let a reader that picks
the best few send less text around the answer. Larger chunks keep more context
together and cost fewer requests.

**Signs it needs changing.** Under `map_reduce` or `skim`, a cost dominated by
the number of requests (`hr_trace_summary()`) points to larger chunks. Under
`retrieve`:

- a right answer that rests on long chunks of unrelated text points to smaller
  chunks;
- an answer split across two chunks, of which `retrieve` picked only one,
  points to larger chunks or to overlap.

**Where the default came from.** The 1200-token default was set when the
segmenters were written and not tuned (`untested`). The recipes set their
own, from 500 (`"needle"`) to 4000 (`"fast"`).

**How to test it.**

```{r}
bench <- sweep(hr_sweep(gr_arm("needle"), list(max_tokens = c(100, 200, 500))))
aggregate(tokens_in ~ param.max_tokens, bench, mean)
```

Under `retrieve`, smaller chunks sent more here: 829 prompt tokens at 100
against 676 at 500. At 100 the report became eight chunks holding 704 tokens,
since each repeats the recipe's 50 tokens of overlap. `retrieve` sent all eight,
because the recipe's `top_k` is 8. At 500 the report became two chunks of 563
tokens. A benchmark on your own reference measures whether the answers change.

### Overlap: `overlap_tokens` {#set-overlap}

**What it controls.** `overlap_tokens` copies the end of each chunk into the
start of the next, so a sentence near a cut is whole in at least one chunk. You
pay for duplicated tokens in every request that carries both chunks. For a
reader that sends every chunk, that means every request (see "Overlap" above).

**Signs it needs changing.** An answer that needs the end of one chunk and the
start of the next, such as a figure in one and its unit in the other, points to
more overlap. A bill that grew with no change in answers points to less.

**Where the default came from.** The default is 0, so no text is sent twice.
It has not been compared with other values (`untested`). Several recipes set
10% of their chunk size.

**How to test it.**

```{r}
bench <- sweep(hr_sweep(gr_arm("needle", list(max_tokens = 100)),
                        list(overlap_tokens = c(0, 20, 50))))
aggregate(tokens_in ~ param.overlap_tokens, bench, mean)
```

At 100-token chunks, 50 tokens of overlap sent 24% more prompt tokens than
none (829 against 669).

### Packing: `packing`, `min_tokens` and `runt_merge` {#set-packing}

**What they control.** These settings decide how units (paragraphs,
sentences, pieces) are packed into chunks under the cap.

- `packing = "greedy"` fills each chunk to `max_tokens` and leaves the
  remainder in the last chunk. `"balanced"` keeps the same number of chunks and
  evens their sizes.
- `min_tokens` merges a chunk smaller than it into the chunk before it.
- `runt_merge = "both"` also merges a first chunk smaller than `min_tokens`
  forward into the second. The backward rule cannot reach a first chunk, since
  nothing comes before it.

**Signs they need changing.** Try `"balanced"` when the last chunk is much
smaller than the others and the reader weighs chunks alike (`retrieve`
scoring, `map_reduce` notes). Try `min_tokens` with `runt_merge = "both"` when
a document's first chunk is only its title, sent as a request of its own.

**Where the defaults came from.** `"greedy"`, `min_tokens = 0` and
`"backward"` reproduce how harnessr packed chunks before these settings
existed. None has been compared with the alternatives (`untested`).

**How to test them.** The chunk sizes show what they do, at no cost:

```{r}
paras <- sprintf("Paragraph %02d reports the year's results in some detail, %s.", 1:25,
                 "with a few more words to give it some length")
long_doc <- gr_ingest(paste(c("Annual review", paras), collapse = "\n\n"))
sizes <- function(...) gr_segment(long_doc, gr_segment_spec("paragraph", ...))$chunks$tokens
sizes(max_tokens = 300)
sizes(max_tokens = 300, packing = "balanced")
```

Greedy packing leaves 197 tokens in the last of three chunks. Balanced packing
makes three of 229, 252 and 225. To test what they do to answers, use arms:

```{r}
bench <- sweep(hr_sweep(gr_arm("needle", list(method = "paragraph", max_tokens = 150)),
                        list(packing = c("greedy", "balanced"))))
aggregate(tokens_in ~ param.packing, bench, mean)
```

The two arms sent different requests here, 901 prompt tokens for
`"balanced"` against 876 for `"greedy"`, because `retrieve` picked chunks of
different sizes. A benchmark on your own reference measures whether answers
change.

### Semantic boundaries: `semantic_threshold` {#set-semantic}

**What it controls.** `semantic_threshold` sets how `semantic` turns the
distances between neighbouring windows into cuts.

- `"percentile"` cuts every gap whose distance reaches the
  `semantic_percentile` of them all. At the default of 90, about one gap in ten
  is cut whether the text changes topic or not.
- `"texttiling"` cuts by depth score, the rule of TextTiling (Hearst 1997). It
  compares the `semantic_window` sentences before each gap with those after
  it and finds the valleys of that similarity. It cuts a valley only when the
  valley is deep by two tests: Hearst's cutoff, and a depth greater than the
  spread of the similarities. A text on one topic then gets at most about one
  cut, and a change of topic gets one.

Both rules use the same embeddings, so they send the same requests.

**Signs it needs changing.** Under `semantic`, chunks that end in the middle
of an argument on a page with no change of subject point to `"texttiling"`.
A long document whose sections run together into a few large chunks under
`"texttiling"` points back to `"percentile"`.

**Where the default came from.** `"percentile"` is the rule `semantic` was
written with. It has not been compared with `"texttiling"` (`untested`).

**How to test it.** Either rule sends the same embedding request, so the first
test is free: count the cuts.

```{r}
by_rule <- sapply(c("percentile", "texttiling"), function(rule) {
  gr_segment(doc, gr_segment_spec("semantic", max_tokens = 1200,
                                  semantic_threshold = rule), client = cl)$extra$boundaries
})
by_rule
```

The example report has a few short sections. `"texttiling"` cuts it twice,
and `"percentile"` three times. To test what the cuts do to answers, use
arms:

```{r}
bench <- sweep(hr_sweep(gr_arm("needle"),
                        list(semantic_threshold = c("percentile", "texttiling"))))
aggregate(tokens_in ~ param.semantic_threshold, bench, mean)
```

Under `"needle"`, whose chunks are at most 500 tokens, the two arms sent
nearly the same prompt tokens here (676 and 675). The packer, which holds
chunks to the cap, sets most of each chunk's size.

### Tables: `table_packing` {#set-tables}

**What it controls.** `table_packing` sets how `paragraph` packs the rows of
a table.

- `"rows"` packs them as it packs any other blocks, so the cap can cut a long
  table anywhere, and only its first chunk carries the header row.
- `"grouped"` packs each table on its own. Every chunk of the table opens with
  the header row, then as many rows as fit.

Under either value, a document's blocks and the chunks of a document with a
table record which table and which rows they hold (`table_id` and
`table_rows`). These columns are provenance only and add nothing to the text.

**Signs it needs changing.** Try `"grouped"` when answers read a figure from
the wrong column of a long table, or cannot say what a row's numbers are. With
it, every chunk of rows carries the column names. Many small tables, each
smaller than a chunk, gain nothing from it.

**Where the default came from.** `"rows"` is how tables were packed before the
setting existed. It has not been compared with `"grouped"` (`untested`).

**How to test it.** The chunks show what it does, at no cost:

```{r}
tab <- tempfile(fileext = ".md")
writeLines(c("# Sales by region", "",
             "| region | units | revenue |", "|---|---|---|",
             sprintf("| region %02d | %d | %d |", 1:30, 100 + 1:30, 1000 + 7 * 1:30)), tab)
tab_doc <- gr_ingest(tab)
by_packing <- lapply(c(rows = "rows", grouped = "grouped"), function(p) {
  gr_segment(tab_doc, gr_segment_spec("paragraph", max_tokens = 150, table_packing = p))
})
lapply(by_packing, function(ch) ch$chunks[, c("chunk_id", "tokens", "table_id", "table_rows")])
sapply(by_packing, function(ch) sum(startsWith(ch$chunks$text, "| region | units |")))
```

Markdown gives the table as one block. Under `"rows"` that block is packed
after the heading and cut wherever the cap falls. No chunk opens with the
header row, and each piece reports the rows of the whole block, `"1-31"`.
Under `"grouped"` every chunk of rows opens with the header, and `table_rows`
gives the rows each chunk holds.

A table from Word or HTML comes one row per block, and then `"rows"` gives
each chunk its own range too. To test what the setting does to answers, run
arms on a reference whose documents have tables. Here `my_tables` is that
reference and `my_client` is your client:

```{r eval = FALSE}
arms <- hr_sweep(gr_arm("thorough", list(method = "paragraph")),
                 list(table_packing = c("rows", "grouped")))
bench <- hr_benchmark(arms, my_tables, runs = 5, client = my_client, split = "dev",
                      scorer = gr_scorer_answer())
hr_report(bench)
```

### Context lines and propositions: `contextual` and `proposition` {#set-contextual}

**What they control.** `contextual` starts each chunk with a line saying where
it sits. The line is built from the file's metadata at no cost, or, with
`context_source = "llm"`, written by a model: one request per chunk, capped at
`context_reply_tokens`, from the first `context_document_tokens` of the
document. `proposition` has a model rewrite the text into standalone
statements, one request per `proposition_batch_tokens` of text.

Both help a chunk retrieved on its own to make sense. Both also put words in
the chunk that are not the document's, which is why harnessr checks quotations
against `source_text`.

**Signs they are needed.** Two signs point to `contextual`: answers that
confuse two sections that say similar things ("revenue rose" in the 2023 and
the 2024 section), and retrieval that picks a chunk whose subject is a
pronoun. Dense factual text where each sentence leans on the one before points
to `proposition`. A segmentation bill that is a large share of the run
(`ctx$trace`) points away from the model-written versions.

**Where the defaults came from.**

- `context_source = "metadata"` was chosen as the source that makes no
  request. It has not been compared with `"llm"`.
- Two rules were set when they were written, and neither was tuned: the
  section path `"llm"` sends, and the test that finds an invented proposition
  (every number in the passage, half its words in the passage or its context).
- `proposition_check = "count"` keeps every proposition, and
  `proposition_context_tokens = 0` sends each batch alone, as before. Neither
  has been compared with the alternatives.
- `proposition_batch_tokens` (900), `context_reply_tokens` (90),
  `context_document_tokens` (1500) and `proposition_reply_tokens` (2000) are
  the values the code had as constants. None was tuned (`untested`).

**How to test them.** Compare `contextual` with the segmenter it builds on:

```{r}
bench <- sweep(hr_sweep(gr_arm("needle", list(max_tokens = 100)),
                        list(method = c("paragraph", "contextual"))))
aggregate(tokens_in ~ param.method, bench, mean)
```

`contextual` sent 81 fewer prompt tokens here. The room it holds back for its
lines makes its chunks smaller, 73 tokens on average against 81, so the
recipe's eight chunks hold less text.

`proposition` and `context_source = "llm"` need a model that writes real
statements, so run them on your own reference and client:

```{r eval = FALSE}
arms <- hr_sweep(gr_arm("needle"), data.frame(
  method = c("paragraph", "contextual", "contextual", "proposition"),
  context_source = c("metadata", "metadata", "llm", "metadata")))
bench <- hr_benchmark(arms, my_reference, runs = 5, client = my_client, split = "dev",
                      scorer = gr_scorer_answer())
aggregate(cbind(correct, usd) ~ param.method + param.context_source, bench, mean)
```

`proposition_check = "drop"` sends the same requests and changes only which
propositions are kept. Before you sweep it, `$extra$propositions_unsupported` on one
segmentation shows what it would drop.

The recipe stores `context_source` even under a segmenter that ignores it. In
every row where it does nothing, give it the value the other rows use, as
above. A row that differs only in an ignored `context_source` would be a
second arm sending the same requests, which `hr_sweep_check()` would then
report.

## Previewing chunks in the Shiny app

The bundled app has a control for every axis: cleaning and OCR, the
segmenter, the reading strategies and the model. For segmentation it also sets
`max_tokens`, overlap and minimum chunk size. Its "Preview chunking" button
shows how the current settings cut the document before you spend anything on
reading. For a segmenter that calls a model, the button says so.

```{r eval = FALSE}
shiny::runApp(system.file("shiny", package = "harnessr"))
```

`GPTREAD_DOC_ROOTS` sets which folders the app can read. Separate folders
with the platform's path separator: a colon, or a semicolon on Windows. Unset,
it defaults to `~/Documents`, falling back to your entire home directory, so
set it before you expose the app to anyone else.

The app opens only the PDF, Word, text, Markdown, HTML and image files under
those folders, never hidden files or hidden folders. It does not offer
`extract` or `screen`, since they read against a protocol. Use `gr_extract()`
and `gr_screen()` instead (`vignette("review")`). A blank cost cap leaves
`hr_options("max_cost_usd")` in force; it does not lift the limit.

## Your own segmenter

`gr_register_segmenter()` adds a segmenter that behaves like the built-ins: it
appears in `gr_segmenters()`, can be named in a recipe, and is held to the same
cap. `new_chunks()` builds the object it must return. `vignette("extending")`
has a worked example.

```{r include = FALSE}
hr_options(old)
```
